utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Sachdeva, to continue with your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President. Good morning, Your Honours, and thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Good morning, General. I trust you rested well last night.

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR GAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Now, yesterday before we closed I was trying to establish your movements in the period 1992 through to 1995, and I wanted to continue with that theme for five minutes or so.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: If I could ask for 65 ter 03503 to be brought up on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: While that's being brought up, General, I take it you're aware of a military magazine called Vojska?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR GAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am. I am aware of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And this -- this is, again, an article from that military magazine, Vojska, and the Prosecution has translated the pertinent part that I want to put to you. Now, do you see on the Serbian version, do you see where you are mentioned? It talks -- the date is 16th of March, 1995, and it talks about -- it mentions you as the artillery school centre commander. Do you see that there firstly on the Serbian version? It's the second paragraph on the left-hand side.

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR GAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And, again, it's -- as I said, it's -- I'm trying to clear up where you were in the period of the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and it says here that - and I'll read from the translation - it says: "This is why the artillery school's centre commander, Colonel Desimir Garovic, a fighter who has spent a year in the field of war in Croatia and Bosnian Krajina with his unit," and then it talks about your interaction in Kragujevac. But I want to ask you again: Why is this Vojska magazine, military magazine, referring to you as having spent a year in the Bosnian Krajina for a year during the war? Is that right or is that incorrect as well?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR GAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This article that I had no influence upon does state some things. It is correct that at the outbreak of the war I was in Banja Luka. I spent there the period we referred to yesterday. As for the rest, it is this journalist's story. I don't know what his motives may have been.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: So now we have two articles - one in a magazine called Glas and another in a military magazine called Vojska which puts you for some time at least -- it suggests that you were active in the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina. And again you deny that; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR GAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I commanded a unit in Bosnia-Herzegovina, as I described yesterday. As for the rest, it is not true. Anything beyond the scope of the presidency's decision for the officers from the area of Serbia and Montenegro to return to their respective areas is incorrect. There were orders in place that I obeyed, and in that period I undertook no activities in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, in this article there is no mention of any year. It can include several years. I don't want to suggest anything in particular, but there is no reference to a year. Perhaps Mr. Sachdeva could provide us with such a reference.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, did you mention a specific year?

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, I did not. It actually refers to the war, and it's established that the war went on from 1992 to 1995. So I simply wanted the General to comment.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: General, may I just --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What is the problem, Mr. -- what's the problem? Why can't he put that? It's for the witness to say whether he was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Your Honours. However, there is no mention of the war between 1992 and 1995. What is mentioned is -- well, a war is mentioned but I don't want to suggest when it began.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: But he's still entitled to put it. It's for the witness to answer. He's not saying that 1992 to 1995 is in the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, Mr. Sachdeva said 1992 to 1995.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, but I don't believe he's saying that that is in the document. Was there a war in Croatia and Bosnia Krajina, 1992 to 1995, Witness?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In that period there was a war in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And were you involved in that war? Did you participate in it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, in that war I participated from the beginning until August. I was in that area until August 1992. As for my participation, I did until the presidency's decision for the transfer of Serbian and Montenegrin officers to be moved into that territory. That happened in May. Therefore, my active participation is limited to -- or by May 1992, for as long as there was the JNA in place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: So you participated as a member of what army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As a member of the JNA.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The JNA. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: General, now I'm slightly confused. In your answer to Mr. President you said that you participated, and I take it you mean 1992, in the war until the beginning of August. This is what you've just said and you clarified it by saying that your active participation was up until May 1992; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR GAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Until May I carried out orders issued by the JNA, as their member. At that moment all officers hailing from Serbia and Montenegro, according to their wishes, may be transferred to the area of Serbia and Montenegro. However, at that time due to the conditions that prevailed we could not take any road or air routes to go to Yugoslavia. Therefore, I was forced to remain there until August without any participation in combat activities or any activities on the part of the VRS. In late August I travelled with my belongings to Serbia, and that's all there is.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: So it's your evidence that after May 1992, in the two months or so that you remained in Banja Luka because you couldn't -- you couldn't get out of the region, you essentially did nothing. You did not participate in combat; you did not carry out orders or adhere to orders from the military formations in Banja Luka. You did nothing; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR GAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In that period one couldn't leave Banja Luka. As any other person working there, I did carry out certain administrative tasks; however, I did not participate in any combat and, in any case, there was no combat in the area of Banja Luka at the time. I did not command any units. The unit I had commanded before that was, indeed, deployed around Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: So now I understand that while you may not have been in combat, you were carrying out administrative tasks for the military, which is the military that you were part of, in Banja Luka from the period May through to August 1992; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR GAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not carrying out their orders. I was there due to a force majeure and no one issued orders to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: General, you are aware that your unit, on the 19th of May, 1992, was incorporated by the newly established army of Republika Srpska and became part of the 1st Krajina Corps. You're aware of that, aren't you?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR GAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am aware of the changes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And so as you remained in Banja Luka through to August carrying out administrative tasks, those administrative tasks would have pertained to the workings of the 1st Krajina Corps, which was headquartered in Banja Luka. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR GAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The tasks I performed had to do with my apartment, had to do with collecting certain documents, so that I would be able to regulate my status once in Serbia. None of the tasks had to do with any combat. None of it had anything to do with combat.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And so in that time you had no contact with the commander Talic, Momir Talic, you had no contact with other members of the Krajina Corps command; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR GAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'd like to tender this article into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We'll admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As P935, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: General, am I right in saying that in 1991 you testified as an expert in a court martial hearing in, I think it was in a VJ court, in a Yugoslav army court; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR GAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my country at the time I don't know of the existence of any court martial court.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: You were not involved in the case against General Trifunovic with regard to the surrendering of the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: -- Varazdin barracks?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let's hear Ms. Isailovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry, Your Honour. One misunderstanding to be lifted. What we're hearing in the B/C/S is something that does not correspond to martial court. What we hear is -- it should be "vojni sud" and the B/C/S is talking about "preki sud," which is something that does not correspond to a martial court and that's why the witness is hearing this and I think that's why there's this misunderstanding right now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you for that clarification.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: So, General, now that the wording has been clarified, were you not involved in a case against -- in the case against General Trifunovic with respect to the Varazdin barracks, the surrendering of those barracks in 1991? You remember that?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR GAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was one of the experts in the proceedings against General Trifunovic as regards artillery.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And may I ask why you have not included that in your biography? Would you not think it's important for the Court to know that you had similarly testified as an artillery expert in a previous case?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR GAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe it was not important. I did not fail to mention that trying to cover up anything but rather out of ignorance.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Now, yesterday when I asked you -- asked you about your unit that you commanded as an artillery commander, you talked about weapons, howitzers, but you said that you did not have mortars in your unit. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR GAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do and that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And while your CV states that you have experience with respect to artillery in general and you -- and you've told the Court that you lecture on issues related to artillery, it's fair to say, is it not, sir, that you are not an expert specific to mortars and the functioning of mortars?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR GAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I taught construction of artillery weaponry and equipment, as part of which we also study the mortar with our cadets. I worked on that for a number of years. As for my familiarity with mortars and other artillery pieces, it is well-founded. Also, with my cadets we carried out live-fire exercises with such weapons. I was training the cadets, trying to equip them with all type of knowledge and skill they might need in operating such weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Yes, General. I'm not suggesting that you don't have knowledge of mortars. But what I'm putting to you is that your career is not solely concerned with the functioning, the firing, the investigation of mortars; isn't that a fair statement?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR GAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: One cannot put it that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Well, either your career -- in your career you solely concerned yourself with mortars or you did not, and as you've already told the Court, you worked on other artillery weapons but you did not confine yourself to the functioning of mortars; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR GAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. I studied other artillery pieces as well and worked with those.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: So as a general observation, General, if the court -- if a court that's deciding on very complicated issues with respect to mortars, if a court hears from a witness that has not spent his career dealing only with mortars as opposed to another witness, expert witness, who has a broad range of knowledge, which expert do you think would --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: No, I don't believe that's a matter for the witness to say, Mr. Sachdeva.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Well, perhaps I can put it in another way.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Would you say that someone who has concerned himself with the functioning and the investigation of mortars throughout his military career and been an advisor to the British military on the specific issue of mortars, the functioning of mortars, how they are fired, where they are deployed, how one investigates mortar incidents, would you be in a better position to provide evidence than that witness?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The witness should not be asked to comment on that. The level of expertise of the witness as against any other witness is a matter that the Court will determine.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: I'm guided, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: General, let me ask you this, then: Have you conducted, have you physically conducted, crater examinations after a 120-millimetre mortar or an 82-millimetre mortar has been fired?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR GAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know which specific crater you have in mind. If you have in mind the craters in Sarajevo, I did not examine those. However, I did examine craters when firing mortars with my cadets and students.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And how many such craters have you examined? I'm not talking about the ones in Sarajevo. You've already given your answer on that. But how many such craters have you -- well, let me ask you this: How many mortar investigations have you yourself conducted in your career?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR GAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: One might say thousands.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And so you are familiar with the investigation when shrapnel has left patterns on the ground. You're familiar with the details of that investigation; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR GAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And in your report you've also mentioned that when one gets to the scene, one of the ways to establish what type of projectile has been fired is to look at the parts that may have been left at the scene, such as the tail-fin. Do you remember putting that in your report? In other words, the tail-fin, the markings on the tail-fin, can give the investigator an idea as to the projectile, the type of projectile, that was used; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR GAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And so when one is trying to establish in an investigation the origin of fire of a mortar, one has to go through certain components. You have to establish the type of round, you'd agree with that, you have to establish the direction of fire, the angle of descent, the charge, to give you an indication of the origin of fire. You agree with those factors?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR GAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the location itself in the crater, one might come across certain indicators, including the elements you mentioned. As for the tail-fin, at the rear there is a marking. It states that it was the basic charge. One can also find data on the producer and calibre of that particular charge. Certain parts of the casing, although very seldom, one can come across certain lettering that usually accompanies rounds. According to the position of the crater and the depth and width of the funnel, one can approximate the calibre. And as for the shrapnel which leave the -- a band around the crater, one can approximate the direction of flight. As for the angle of descent, that can only be calculated. To determine the type of charge, that is impossible. And it is impossible to determine any other parameters based on which we could come to a more accurate calculation of the trajectory.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Thank you for that long answer. I'm going to get to those details later. But I want to stick to the type of projectile that may have been used. So, for example, you could see -- you could have a tail-fin which suggests that the tail-fin is from an M-52 mortar or an M-75 mortar. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR GAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A tail-fin can only tell you something about the calibre of the round, but it does not point to any particular model of weapon, whether it is an M-75 or any other. A round can be fired from several types of mortars.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And once you establish the calibre from the tail-fin, you then, in your investigation, you then would look at the firing tables that pertain to that particular calibre. So if it's an M-52, you look at the firing tables related to an M-52. If it is an M-74, you similarly look at the firing tables related to an M-74. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR GAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is not right. By using the round itself, one cannot determine which model and which weapon it was, whether it is an M-52 or M-75. The round cannot tell you which mortar had fired it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: I'm not suggesting that the round will tell you which mortar. But if you have the tail-fin that suggests the calibre of the round and you want to establish, in your investigation you want to establish the possible range with other factors as well, you would in your investigation, as part of your investigation, you would refer to the firing tables for that round. In other words, if you've established that it's an M-52 calibre, you would look at the firing tables for an M-52. That's all I'm saying. I'm not saying it gives you -- I'm not saying it undercuts anything else you have to do in an investigation, but at least that would be a starting point. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR GAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would not. A tail-fin can tell you none of those things. It can only tell you about the calibre and that is it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: General, I think that you're not understanding me. Let's take the starting point that the tail-fin can tell you the calibre of the round. We agree on that. You've just said so. I agree with you.

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR GAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Now, as we've discussed and as you've told the Court, to establish the likely firing position, you have to go through a certain amount of steps in your investigation. You agree with that?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR GAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And you agree that with each calibre, whether it's an M-52 or an M-74, there are firing tables, written, completed firing tables from, for example, the JNA, that refer to those calibres. You agree with that?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR GAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. One of such firing tables I have before me.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And so what I'm saying is, and I'm not saying this information gives you all you want in your investigation, but at least as a starting point when you are trying to do your investigation you would -- one would refer to the firing tables of the calibre of the round that you found at the scene. So if it was an M-52, you would refer to the firing tables, the produced firing tables, of an M-52. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR GAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, Mr. Prosecutor, one cannot establish what kind of weapon fired a projectile based on the type of projectile, whether it's an M-52 or an M-75, because both types of weapons can fire the same calibre shell. The tail-fin we can find where the crater is can come from two types of shell, a light shell and a heavy shell. They do not differ in any of their elements, so it's impossible to tell from a tail-fin whether the shell in question is a light one or a heavy one. The tail-fin does not allow us to establish that --

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR GAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- if you can believe someone who has fired hundreds of thousands of projectiles.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: General, I feel we're getting more complicated than we need to. I'm simply making this one suggestion to you. Let me try and put it this way: For an M -- I see has you're referring to a book. If you could just -- thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: If you are -- General, if you are going to refer to a book, then you must inform the Court.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: You agree that there are firing tables, as I said, written, produced, JNA firing tables for an M-52 calibre. You agree with that?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR GAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And you agree that there are also firing tables for an M-74?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR GAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Similarly, there are also firing tables for an M-75.

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR GAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Now, you've told the Court, and in fact Mr. Tapuskovic has said that in your -- in your report and while producing your report, you reviewed the evidence in this case; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR GAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: I take it, then, you reviewed the reports, documents, the witness evidence, for the Markale incident.

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR GAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Did you review the Bosnian police report for that incident?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR GAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And did you also review the report by the UN military observer, Mr. Konings? Do you remember reviewing that report?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR GAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have reviewed all the documents disclosed by the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Then you -- you know then that the calibre of the round that was fired at the Markale market -- well, what is the calibre of the round that was fired there? Do you know?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR GAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to the documents disclosed, it was a light mine, 120 millimetres, M-75. Sorry, a light shell, M-62.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Are you sure it wasn't an M-74, General?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR GAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just a minute, please. Just a minute. I copied it down. A light shell, M-62, 120 millimetres, P-2.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Sir, I suggest to you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: General, would you tell us what book you're referring to? You're not prohibited from doing it, but let us know what is it that you are using.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the report I wrote.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: It's your report. I see. Okay.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: General, you reviewed the report of Mr. Higgs, did you not?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR GAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And therefore I take it with that report and also with the Bosnian police report that you reviewed, you know that the round that was fired was from an M-74 batch.

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR GAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to what it says, yes, it's a light shell.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And I just make the point that in your report, when you have included firing tables and firing graphs, they all pertain to the M-76; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR GAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't understand you. M-76? There is no M-76. There is M-75, if we're talking about mortars. The calibre is M-75.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Well, in the translation of the report that I have, you have a firing graph that indicates, at least it's entitled the 120-millimetre mortar, light mortar, M-76, and the firing tables that you have provided pertain to an M-75. And I make the point that nowhere is there any information related to an M-74.

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR GAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If this is a mortar, the title is "120-millimetre, M-75" for a mortar, and that's how it is in my report. There's no 76.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: There's also no M-74, is there?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR GAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, there isn't, because the difference between these two mortars is negligible. It doesn't influence any ballistic element. For that reason I felt it unnecessary to deal with both. They are the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: There is a difference, is there not?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR GAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The difference does not affect ballistic conditions. It does not affect targeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: There's a difference enough so as to warrant two different tables, one for an M-74 and one for an M-75; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR GAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In military libraries I found firing tables for M-75. Those were the ones I used. There's no difference. I didn't find the other one.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: With respect, please just answer the question. There is a difference that warrants two different tables, one for an M-75 and one for an M-74. You may not have found the M-74, but there is a difference, is there not?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR GAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not in terms of ballistics, not in terms of ballistics. As regards the trajectory and the impact of the projectile, no, there isn't. No difference.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And what about the ranges?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR GAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The ranges depend on the type of projectile, the projectile that was used. If it's a heavy shell then it's one range, and if it's a light shell it's another range. It depends on the weight of the projectile, not on the mortar, whether it's an M-74 or an M-75.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Now, yesterday when you were speaking about the transport of mortars, you said that a 120-millimetre mortar, according to your knowledge of the regulations, needs to be transported by a motor vehicle. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR GAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Isn't it also correct, sir, that the JNA provides for the transport of 120-millimetre mortars by, in addition to a motor vehicle or in the alternative, by a mule or more than one mule; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR GAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and that refers to a 120-millimetre M-52 mortar. The JNA did not have mules or other kinds of pack animals.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: But yesterday when you were asked to give information as to how mortars are transported, you did not mention the mule, when in fact it is provided for in the rules, is it not?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR GAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but to the best of my knowledge, and I know for certain, the JNA had neither mules nor horses. There were never mules in that area. They only used horses and they didn't have those.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Which area are you talking about, sir?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR GAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm talking about the mountainous areas around Sarajevo, the mountainous areas of the SFRY, the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. Everywhere in the former SFRY, in fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: It's important to be specific about the area. I take it you weren't with the VRS or the JNA stationed in Mount Trebevic, were you?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR GAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I lived in Sarajevo for 15 years, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: That's not what I'm asking. I'm asking you that from the period 1992 through to 1995, you were not with the VRS, the SRK, or the JNA stationed on Mount Trebevic or in Sarajevo at all, were you?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR GAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: If I could ask for 65 ter 03394. Perhaps, Mr. President, I'll come back to this because I have to establish what page. I know the paragraph. And I can do that in the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: General, I'm sorry, I'm going to move on to another topic now. General, I want to talk to you about the aspect of your report where you described the killing range of a 120-millimetre mortar. Do you remember that information in your report?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR GAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Firstly, we can agree that, and as you've said yesterday, that the main purpose of a mortar, the design of a mortar, is to maximise the killing of enemy personnel or the harassment of enemy personnel. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR GAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, not according to the definition we had in our rules of combat. It's intended for the destruction of enemy manpower. It doesn't mention harassment. It's combat and the aim is to destroy enemy manpower. There are other tasks also which I will not go into, but they do not refer to manpower.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Well, that's fine. We can go with that. So the main purpose is to destroy, to kill, in other words, enemy personnel. That's right?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR GAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Now, in your report you talk about -- you give a figure of the amount of shrapnel, the fragments that -- the amount of fragments there are when a mortar explodes and you've given that figure of 3.500 or so. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR GAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And you go on to say that only about 250 to 300 of that 3.500 are -- cause lethal injuries. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR GAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: So by my calculation, and I'm not a mathematician by any means; however, but that would render, in terms of the purpose of a mortar, that would, with your figures, that would render the mortar some roughly 10 per cent effective. In other words, if only 250 out of the 3.500 shrapnel pieces are lethal, then it renders a mortar pretty much 90 per cent ineffective, by your calculation?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR GAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The calculations I presented are based on experimental methods. Mathematical methods were used to prove how many pieces of shrapnel there were in total. It's 2.5 to 3.000 pieces. And of that total number, 10 per cent is lethal. Ten per cent have the kinetic energy of about 100 joule or more, which is sufficient to kill a human being. That's why these figures are what they are.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And then beyond that, how many of those pieces would cause casualties, not necessarily lethal casualties but casualties?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR GAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The range of the pieces of shrapnel from a mortar is 150 metres from the epicentre at the most. But in view of the fact that when a shell explodes, the pieces of shrapnel are dispersed in a sphere.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, it says 150 metres. The witness said 50 metres. The expert witness said 50 metres, whereas the transcript says 150.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you for that clarification.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Did the witness say that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, I take Mr. Tapuskovic's word, but I'll ask the witness. Witness, what did you say, 150 metres or 50 metres?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I said 50 metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: General, I suggest to you that the casualty range for a 120-millimetre mortar is up to 190 to 200 metres from the centre of the explosion.

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR GAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of any such mortars. That might refer to a bomb dropped from a plane. But as for mortars, it's what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Up to 200 metres if people are in the vicinity of a -- within 200 metres of a 120-millimetre mortar shell that explodes into thousands of fragments, I suggest to you that there will be people beyond the 50- or 70-metre mark that would sustain injuries, not necessarily lethal but would sustain injuries. Do you agree with that or not?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR GAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Now I want to move on to the issue of sound which you spoke about yesterday. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR GAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And you said that somebody could hear a 120-millimetre mortar being fired if that person was up to 5 to 6 kilometres away from the firing position. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR GAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And so if somebody was a kilometre away, then it's virtually impossible that if a mortar was fired a kilometre away from, let's say, a UN observer, it would be impossible if that mortar had been fired for him not to have heard that. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR GAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Tapuskovic, you may recall, spoke to you about the position of 2.400 metres from the Markale market. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR GAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And I think you're aware --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, when I asked the witness about these things, I was speaking in general and I was speaking about the possible -- a possible distance of 2.400 metres. I didn't mention Markale. I said if the distance is 2.400 metres, what's the situation. I didn't mention Markale then.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Sachdeva.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Witness, let me put this scenario to you. You have an observer in a certain location and then a kilometre away, let's say hypothetically, a kilometre away a mortar, a 120-millimetre mortar has been fired. Are you with me on this for the moment?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR GAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And your evidence is that ordinarily when the mortar has been fired, that observer would have heard, or should have heard, the 120-millimetre mortar being fired; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR GAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He should have heard. It's certain that that person would have heard it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: If, however, there was a mountain or a hill or other similar relief features between the observer and the firing position, it's possible; in fact, I suggest to you that the sound would be muffled or, in fact, non-existent and therefore make it more difficult for that person to hear the mortar being fired. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR GAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Mountains and elevations have an impact on the intensity of the sound, but at those distances the intensity of the sound is sufficient for the firing to be heard.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Well, you've agreed that the mountain or the relief features would affect the sound. You agree with that, don't you? Of course it's obvious that a mountain or a hill would have an impact on the sound, it would muffle the sound, deflect the sound. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR GAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mountainous areas do have an impact on the sound, but there is an echo effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: General, I just want you to follow my questions. Okay, you agree with that. And so what I'm suggesting to you is that it would be --

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR GAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: -- it is therefore, in that situation, one cannot guarantee that somebody would have heard the firing of a mortar. In other words, it is less likely for that person to have heard the mortar being fired.

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR GAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It depends on the distance. At small distances one can hear it; at longer distances, it's possible that the sound would not be heard.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: In any case, you agree that the sound is deflected and the sound is different, it's muffled. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR GAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Of course you spoke about these rather technical sound devices. Do you remember speaking about that yesterday?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR GAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And of course for those sound devices to work, they would have had to have been installed in the military, in the theatre. That's obviously correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR GAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And you also spoke about the radar, the Cymbeline radar. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR GAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And again I put the same question to you, that -- well, let me first go back to what you said. You gave in an answer to Mr. Tapuskovic that the radars are established or set up in areas where -- in certain areas where it is presumed fire will be coming from. So it depends on where you set the radars, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR GAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: So if a mortar is fired from the south and the radar is set up to cover the north or the east, it wouldn't obviously pick up the mortar being fired from the south. That's a logical conclusion.

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR GAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If there's only one radar, then the conclusion is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And for -- similarly, for these radars to be effective, for someone to establish the firing position, that person has to catch the times when both the lower elevation, the lower beam, and the higher beam are cut in the trajectory of the firing projectile; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR GAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: So, again, it depends on what elevation, what level, the radar is set.

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR GAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The radars are set from 0 elevation to plus 70 degrees.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: But, General, it's possible, is it not, that a radar could be set at such an elevation that that would not enable it to catch the projectile cutting both beams. In other words, a projectile could fly underneath the level set by the radar, the beam set by the radar.

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR GAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: You're saying that it's not possible for a projectile to fly below the level of a radar beam?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR GAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A mortar projectile can never fly below the radar beam. It has to be cut by the radar beam.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: But does it not depend on what beam -- at what level the radar has been set? It surely must depend on that.

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR GAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Radars are designed in such a way as to operate in all conditions. Their elevation settings provide for mountainous terrain, as well as flatlands, elevations, depressions. Literally speaking it is impossible for a mortar round to be fired without the Cymbeline recording it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: I'm asking you to answer the question. Does it not depend on the level, the elevation level, set -- the level elevation that's been set with the radar? It depends on that. Whether it's unlikely that it was set that way or not, I'm just asking you to agree with the possibility or to agree that it depends on the level set by the radar.

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR GAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A radar elevation setting provides for any projectile to be detected.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Do you know what the elevation settings were in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR GAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not familiar with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Do you know where the radar -- where the radars were located in Sarajevo during the war?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR GAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to the documents I had at my disposal, they were at the airport, around the Sarajevo airport. It's a flat area.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And the airport is pretty much the other end of town from Mount Trebevic, is it not?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR GAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Now, the other factor about radar, and you've talked about how they are very accurate, but the accurate readings depend on the person at the computer watching at the time the projectile cuts both the beams, and for that person then to identify the location and then therefore to calculate -- from those measurements, calculate the origin of fire. So it depends on the efficiency of the human person being there at the time these beams are cut, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR GAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Radar precision depends on the type of instrument. As for the calculations, it depends on the crew. The crew has no impact on the precision of recorded elements.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: But the crew has to identify when those beams have been cut, at what time those beams have been cut, and the crew has to record that information for the eventual calculations to be established; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR GAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the radar screen one registers the data as to what the beams were cut and what the parameters were at that moment. It stays on the screen long enough for the crew to be able to use it. That is entirely independent of the crew.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Well, when you say one registers the data, by that I mean -- by that I take it you mean the person who is reviewing the screen at the time. In other words, it depends on the efficiency of a human watching that computer and recording the data. That's all I'm putting to you.

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR GAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Registration is automatic, with no influence on the part of the crew.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And that information, how is that information recorded and passed on, and how are the calculations made?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR GAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The information recorded is introduced into the computer. Then the crew undertakes certain calculations and the final results are the exact coordinates of firing. All that takes less than one minute.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Now, you told the Court with respect to the prerecording of targets -- you remember speaking about the prerecording of targets?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR GAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And I want to ask you that, as an artillery person, you surely cannot be telling the Court that this procedure whereby a target -- the coordinates of a target are recorded down in a log and then kept for future use, you're saying that that does not occur.

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR GAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said yesterday, the first time I encountered the term of "prerecorded target" was when reading this documentation. In artillery units there is no way or practice for targets to be prerecorded and kept in some sort of archives or for any other future use.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Are you saying that armies, including the JNA or the VRS, did not have target lists that were pre-prepared, that had been pre-prepared? Are you saying those things do not exist?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR GAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: During reconnaissance enemy activity is recorded. It is also recorded in any given area the enemy is of such and such strength and type. However, such data is not useful for artillery units to carry out firing. Such data is not used in artillery.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: I'll get to the use in a moment. But I want you to first agree with me that a military target, for example, in the city of Sarajevo like a barracks or something of that character, the coordinates of that target can be recorded and kept as a target in a list of targets. That's possible, is it not?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR GAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is possible to register those coordinates.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And you agree with me that the city of Sarajevo, with its several identifying features -- for example, you have -- you know that there's a cathedral in the central of town. You agree with that, that there's a cathedral there?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR GAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And for a mortar crew who hail from the Sarajevo region, they can use that identifying feature, such as the cathedral spire, or other similar features, to be able to establish coordinates in a much easier and quicker fashion than in an open battlefield. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR GAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Knowing the coordinates of a cathedral or another building does not contribute to any quicker calculation on the part of the crew. It bears no importance irrespective of the type of building. What I wanted to state also was that they never targeted the cathedral.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: I didn't suggest that in my question. Let me put a scenario to you. You have a mortar crew that has at the beginning, let's say, beginning of the conflict, beginning of the Sarajevo conflict, fired a couple of mortars into the city with a direct line of sight, and through the firing of those mortars they have adjusted their rounds until they have established almost a direct fire for the target they want to hit. And once they have established those coordinates, those coordinates are recorded. You're following what I'm saying, I take it?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR GAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And that mortar crew has its mortar with the base plates dug in and that mortar stays there for three or four or even -- three or four months or even a year. And then that mortar crew goes back, let's say, in a year's time to the mortar in the same location as it was when it fired those initial rounds and it takes out its target list and it has those coordinates that represent the target that it hit a year ago. Are you now saying that that information, the same crew with the same mortar location, that information is not useful?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR GAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This scenario is rather odd. The data that the crew might use --

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: General, sorry, before you answer, I don't want you to comment on the scenario. I'm just saying that if that scenario were to be the case, you cannot tell the Court that that information, those target coordinates, would not be useful to that mortar crew, I suggest to you.

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR GAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise, sir. Such data is completely useless to the crew.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: General, we have heard in this case an expert who has come here and given evidence, an expert on mortars, who has told the Court in his report and also during the evidence that the prerecording of targets in Sarajevo with a military situation that pretty much remained static throughout the three to four years - in other words, mortar positions weren't moved throughout that time period - that the prerecording of targets most certainly increases the accuracy of the mortar crew that is firing into the city. And you disagree with that expert's evidence.

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR GAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I disagree, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And even if one were to take into account the variations with respect to the weather, with respect to atmospheric conditions, those coordinates would still assist -- enable the mortar crew to fire the round, maybe not necessarily the exact place where the initial round was fired, but at least within 10 to 15 metres of that first round. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR GAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If one calculates in all of the weather and ballistic conditions at the moment prior to the firing and if all the parameters impacting the flight of the projectile be taken into account, such coordinates of any given building in Sarajevo, with the weather, ballistic conditions, and all of the other types of influence impacting the flight of the projectile, do assist us in acquiring an impact approximate to the coordinates prerecorded. Without any of those it is not possible, however.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Well, that's the answer. That's what I was putting to you, and I take it you agree with that. Now, yesterday you spoke about observers as well. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR GAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And Mr. Tapuskovic talked to you about the use of observers with indirect and direct fire? Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR GAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Would you agree with me, General, that if a mortar crew has direct line of sight of a target that it intends to hit, in other words, almost using the mortar like a rifle, notwithstanding the parabolic trajectory, that target could be hit without the use of an observer. In other words, it's not necessary to have an observer if it has a direct line of sight.

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR GAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mortars never fire directly irrespective of whether they can see the target or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: General, that's why I put in my qualification about the curve. I'm not suggesting that it's a straight, direct fire like a rifle or a tank. But what I'm suggesting to you is that if a mortar battery crew has -- is positioned, for example, on a hill and can see down into the valley and can see a target, it can then try and engage that target with or without the use of an observer. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR GAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understood you and I've given my answer. Due to the parabolic trajectory, a mortar cannot target and hit a target directly. The parabolic trajectory makes it necessary for all of the elements to be calculated as if one were targeting indirectly. Irrespective of whether we can see the target or not, we still have to factor in the parabolic trajectory. It is unimportant whether they can see the target from the place of firing or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: General, are you really saying that the fact that a mortar crew can see a target is unimportant in their -- in what they try to do? Are you saying that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: No, he didn't say that, Mr. Sachdeva. I think you should move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: I think he said it in the last sentence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You say that "Irrespective of whether we can see the target or not, we still have to factor in the parabolic trajectory. It is unimportant whether they can see the target from the place of firing or not." So the parabolic trajectory is, for him, key, crucial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, there's something I don't understand very well because when the person firing can see the target, I think there is some confusion here. What is the person firing supposed to do and what is the observer supposed to do? Because the observer tells the person firing where the target is located, where the first shell has fallen, and what needs to be done to improve the firing range. But when the person firing can see the target, he is in the same position as the observer. So I don't understand the observer who can see the target, the person firing who can see the target, whether he sees the target or doesn't see it, that that doesn't make any difference. I don't understand the rationale here.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The person firing a round at the mortar has the same role as an observer that might be to the front, without being able to see the piece. Therefore, cooperation is the same between the two. They conduct the same activities. The nature of the parabolic curve is such that it does not provide for direct targeting. One cannot turn the mortar tube directly on to the target. The crew member can be the observer and vice versa. However, the parabolic trajectory always needs to be factored in. I don't know whether I was clear enough.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, you were clear, but I think the issue hinges on the word "directly," because when the person firing is an observer, he might not be able to reach the target first time round, and after having missed the first time, then the second time he is better able to direct the shot, the mortar, and will be able to reach the target in the end because he can observe and see what's happening. He won't hit the target the first time round, but the next time round he might be able to. What do you think about this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. For the next round he needs to enter certain corrections, which is also something done by an observer who cannot see the firing position. Therefore, the action is the same in both cases. There is a correction of targeting, whether they see the target or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Sachdeva.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: General, we were talking -- you were speaking yesterday about the phenomenon of the tail-fins in the -- sticking into the ground at the explosion site. Do you remember talking about that?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR GAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but I did not talk specifically about tail-fins plunging into the ground. I did talk about the issue of tail-fins in general.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: But generally we can agree that if a tail-fin is found in the ground in the explosion site, generally it means that it was fired -- or the mortar came in from a further distance at a higher speed.

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR GAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A tail-fin is found in the immediate vicinity of an explosion. It can tell us something about the calibre but it cannot tell us anything about the place and direction of firing or about the distance.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: So what I'm suggesting to you is that if the tail-fin is found in the ground, as it was in one of the incidents that you have reviewed in Livanjska Street, the general assumption - I'm not saying that it's definite - the general assumption is that it came -- therefore the mortar came from a further distance, the mortar was fired from a further distance. It's the same physics with respect to the depth of the fuse, the funnel that you spoke about yesterday, the fuse furrow. If you have a deeper funnel or if the tail-fin is embedded in the ground, it suggests, it's an indication, that the mortar was fired from a further distance and therefore had a higher velocity. This is what you said yesterday.

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR GAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yesterday I said, and I reiterate, that only the depth of the funnel can tell us anything about the distance from which that round was fired. The tail-fin does not provide us with any information on the distance of firing. I repeat: It doesn't tell us anything about the distance of firing.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And you never have come across an incident where a tail-fin had been stuck -- had been stuck in the ground at the explosion site?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR GAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yesterday I presented some data to you. During a projectile explosion, the tail-fin is ejected. Depending on the speed of descent, the forces ejecting the tail-fin and the speed of movement of the tail-fin annul each other. Depending on the size of one or the other force, the ejection distance is greater or lesser from the place of explosion. In order for a tail-fin to bury itself in the ground, one needs to have the speed of the projectile greater than 650 metres, or around 700 metres per second. In such circumstances that tail-fin can be found buried in the crater. However, all speeds of descent are in the range of 3 to 400 metres and it is therefore natural to suppose that the tail-fin is never buried in the ground. It also depends on the hardness of the surface. In my previous experience as a lecturer, I have never come across a tail-fin buried in the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: But you're aware that the incident at Livanjska Street, the tail-fin was found in the ground and you are also aware, are you not, that in the first Markale incident, the tail-fin was found in the ground. So therefore I suggest to you, as Mr. Higgs has stated to the Court here, that it is possible for a tail-fin to be found in the ground, and that generally indicates that the firing was from a farther distance and the speed was higher.

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR GAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no comment as to how those tail-fins ended up in the crater. It would be unjust of me.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And if we talk about the depth of the crater, which you were speaking about --

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I'm going to move on to a new subject, perhaps it's time for a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. We'll take the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Sachdeva.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: General, before I move on to my next topic, I just want to ask you with respect to one of the answers you gave, and this is at line 12 on page 28, you said: "What I want to state also was that they never targeted the cathedral." Do you remember saying that?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR GAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Given the fact that you were not with the VRS in Sarajevo during the war and during the indictment period, how do you know they never targeted the cathedral?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR GAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the documents I studied I found no cases of fire on that building.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: So what you're saying is from the material that you reviewed with respect to the mortar incidents in the indictment, you've come to the conclusion that they never targeted the cathedral. I suggest to you, sir, of course you don't know if they ever intended to target the cathedral, do you?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR GAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know according to the documents. I know what I said. I don't know about their intentions.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. Now, I was about to move on to the -- what you were speaking about yesterday with respect to the depth of the crater and the depth of the funnel. Do you remember talking about that?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR GAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And you said that if there was a shallow crater, a shallow funnel, according to your expertise, that then indicated that the shell was fired from charges, one or two, in other words, from a lesser distance, or that it could have been a static explosion. Am I correct in my understanding of your evidence?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR GAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Of course, General, the depth or shallowness of the crater depends on the surface that the shell lands on, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR GAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the characteristics of the soil, of the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And so one could have a shell that has landed on hard ground, such as asphalt or a road, and it could produce a shallow crater, but that would not necessarily mean that the shell was fired from a lesser distance or, indeed, that it was a static explosion.

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR GAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The characteristics of all kinds of ground and their hardness is something where one knows what the depth of the crater will be in view of the range. So the same projectile landing on soil or on asphalt and so on would not produce the same depth of crater. But in every case the shallowness of the crater in relation to the type of ground speaks of the velocity and range of the projectile.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: But, General, you cannot subtract or take away the factor, the very huge factor, I suggest, of the hardness of the ground and therefore I want you to agree with me that if you have a shallow crater on hard ground, it does not necessarily mean that the shell was fired from a lesser distance or that it was a static explosion. You surely have to agree with that.

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR GAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot agree with that. A shallow crater on hard ground means that the projectile arrived at a slow velocity and it produced a small crater. If the projectile arrived at a high velocity, then the crater would be larger. Experiments have shown that low-velocity projectiles create small craters and high-velocity projectiles create deeper craters. Here I exclude those projectiles that burrow deeper into the ground, which are slowed down.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: As a general conclusion, that is -- I would agree with you that the depth of the crater obviously indicates the velocity of the shell. However, you have to factor in the hardness of the ground, do you not?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR GAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is factored in, yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Now, you've told the Court that you were not in Sarajevo during the conflict and therefore I take it that the day the incident occurred at Markale, you weren't at the site, were you?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR GAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Unlike the Bosnian investigators, unlike the UN investigators, you were not able to conduct an in situe investigation; you did not take measurements at the scene, did you?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR GAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: General, are you an expert in photogrametrics?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR GAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was the commander of a unit that dealt with that. I completed certain training for that job and I also taught on topographical geodetic work at the military academy, so I think I am familiar with that subject matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: I didn't ask you whether you are familiar. I asked you whether you're an expert in photogrametrics, in the field of photogrametrics. Are you or are you not an expert in that field?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR GAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nobody has ever asked me to produce an expert report in that field.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And no one's ever asked you to because you're not an expert in that field, are you? It's a simple question: Are you an expert or are you not?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR GAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm acquainted with that field, I'm familiar with it. I have done that for the needs of the army. I feel I am qualified to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Why didn't you include that in your biographical data, in your CV? Why is that not indicated?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR GAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there's a lot of things that I'm qualified to do which I have not included because I felt them to be of lesser importance.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: So what you're saying is that when you come to the court and give your conclusions about measurements based on your familiarity with photogrametrics, according to you that's not of importance to include that in your CV. Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR GAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not include it in my CV because I was not asked to. I didn't think that every detail of my work ought to be included, so I probably omitted to include that. But I am familiar with that field.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Well, of course not every detail, but this is a detail that you have given lengthy evidence on and you have not included it in your CV. Why didn't you do that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let's move on, Mr. Sachdeva.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Now, when you spoke yesterday about the respective sketches and diagrams, do you remember talking about those diagrams yesterday with respect to the Markale incident?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR GAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And I recall that you took issue with the measurements of the height of the building. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR GAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I pointed out that the height of the building cannot be established exactly, but I accepted the measurement provided in the documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: You did not accept the measurement, the distance from the explosion crater to the foot of the building. You said that the measurements were wrong in that sketch. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR GAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: General, do you really think that your analysis or your measurements are more accurate than the measurements made by trained investigators who were at the scene at the day of the explosion, not only Bosnian investigators but also UN investigators? Are you asking the Court to take your measurements over those measurements made physically with measuring tapes?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR GAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I consider that the measurements I presented are approximately correct and that they are more correct than the measurements entered into those sketches. I'm not going into who provided those measurements.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: So your evidence is that your measurements are more correct than --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let's move on, Mr. Sachdeva. You're just repeating the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Very well. If I could have Exhibit P254 brought up on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Witness, you remember seeing this sketch yesterday, I take it?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR GAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: This sketch is an illustration of the calculation of the angle of descent. You agree with that? Whether it's the right calculation or not, but this sketch is being used to calculate the angle of descent. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR GAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And this is how the angle of descent is calculated.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Nowhere on this sketch is it indicated that it's -- nowhere on this sketch is it indicated the direction of the projectile. That's not contained in this sketch, is it?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR GAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: It does not say that the shell came from the north, from the south, from the east, from the west. It's simply a sketch used to determine the angle of descent.

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR GAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would not agree. The vertical line on the left-hand side of the drawing suggests that that is the building across from the market. It's a thick vertical line so it suggests the building, the market building, in fact, which says that the projectile came from the south.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Does it say on this sketch -- does it say on this sketch that that vertical line represents a building? Does it say that on this sketch?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR GAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it doesn't say that, but that was my understanding of the sketch.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: So it is your assumption that the vertical line represents a building; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR GAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: It could also be, could it not, that this is a standard sketch used by investigators to demonstrate how the angle of descent is calculated, and that that vertical line has nothing to do whatsoever with the position of the building. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR GAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a possibility. Not necessarily so, but it's a possibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Now, on a general level, when one is investigating what happened at a mortar explosion -- at a mortar explosion and one has an indication that the mortar that was used was a 120-millimetre mortar, and if one is attempting to establish which side fired that mortar, one of the factors that you would have to establish is whether the army that you presume is responsible, whether it be the ABiH or whether it be the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps, one would have to establish whether they had in their arsenal 120-millimetre mortars. Do you agree with that statement?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR GAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: One must establish whether they had a certain type of weapon, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I could ask for -- it's 65 ter 03395.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Now, General, you see a document on your screen and this document is from the 1st Sarajevo Mountain -- 1st Sarajevo Mechanised Brigade on the 5th of August, 1995, and it is, as you can see, a report on the receipt of materials -- material, supplies and funds. I suggest to you, and I don't think that this is disputed, that the 1st Sarajevo Mechanised Brigade controlled the territory, part of the VRS territory, in the area where the market was located, in other words in the Serb confrontation lines. And I want you to look down the list and you will see there in the first line that it is reported that in the month of July 1995, the 1st Sarajevo Mechanised Brigade received from the 27th Logistics Base 160 pieces of 120-millimetre mortar. I just want you to agree with me that that's what's indicated in this document.

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR GAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I agree that that's what the document says.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'd like to tender this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As P936, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Yesterday, when you were shown the picture of the crater, do you remember seeing a picture of the crater - I think it was Exhibit P264 - and you agreed that the direction of fire was roughly 175 degrees. You said, in fact, if I can remember, that it was impossible to make a mistake on the direction of fire from that crater. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR GAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember seeing the photograph and I said that the general direction of arrival was as shown.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And when talking about the Markale incident, your conclusions, if I can put it that way, were that because of the shallowness of the crater, it indicated that the shell was fired from a closer distance or that there was a static explosion. Those are your conclusions, aren't they?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR GAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Now, of course, given the fact that you did not go to the scene on the day of the explosion and conduct your own investigation and so your conclusions are based upon, at least as I see it from the evidence you've given and from your report, on the shallowness of the crater, you would not have seen -- if, indeed, there had been a static explosion, you did not see any secondary explosive marks on the ground that would have been -- that would have existed if there had been a static explosion, did you?

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR GAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: In fact --

utterances.speaker: DESIMIR GAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I explain?

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: If I can just continue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, let him give the explanation. I'd like to hear it. You wanted to explain? Yes, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Your Honour, I based my expert report on the documents disclosed by the Prosecution which we had at our disposal. All the calculations were made in the documents in order to determine the approximate angle of descent, the direction of arrival, and the angle at which the projectile could have flown over the building in order to explode where it did, and that's why I used the photogrametric method.
